key_features.classic_presentation: ONSET: SUDDEN onset within hours to 1-2 days. Acute presentation. Often follows sick contacts or contaminated food/water. LOCATION: PERIUMBILICAL or DIFFUSE throughout abdomen. NOT localized to one quadrant. Cramping moves around. DURATION: Episodes last hours to days. Individual cramps last seconds to minutes. Typically resolves within 3-7 days. CHARACTER: CRAMPY, DIFFUSE pain. INTERMITTENT (comes and goes in waves), NOT constant. Dull cramping quality. AGGRAVATING: Eating may worsen cramping initially. Movement during cramp uncomfortable. Bowel movements trigger cramping. RELIEVING: Defecation provides TEMPORARY relief. Bowel movements reduce cramping. Symptoms improve with hydration and rest. TIMING: INTERMITTENT waves of cramping with bowel movements. Cramps come and go. NOT constant. SEVERITY: 3-6/10, mild to moderate cramping. DIARRHEA is PREDOMINANT symptom (more prominent than pain). ASSOCIATED SYMPTOMS: DIARRHEA (3+ watery stools/day) as main symptom, NAUSEA AND VOMITING (often BEFORE or WITH diarrhea), low-grade fever or none, hyperactive bowel sounds. APPETITE often PRESERVED (unlike appendicitis with severe anorexia). KEY POSITIVES: Diarrhea predominant, diffuse cramping, sick contacts, appetite preserved, hyperactive bowel sounds. KEY NEGATIVES: Pain MIGRATING to right lower quadrant (RLQ) suggests appendicitis. SEVERE LOCALIZED tenderness with guarding rules out. Pain WITHOUT diarrhea uncommon.

includes.patient_friendly: all at once or very quickly

red_flags: Severe dehydration (dry mucous membranes, decreased urine output, orthostatic hypotension) - needs IV fluids
Bloody diarrhea with high fever >102°F - invasive bacterial infection (Shigella, Salmonella, E. coli), may need antibiotics
Severe abdominal pain with peritoneal signs - suggests perforation or alternative diagnosis, not simple gastroenteritis
Immunocompromised patients or infants - higher risk of severe dehydration and complications
